# Problem 1

```{r}
data("ny_noaa")

glimpse(ny_noaa)

ny_noaa |>
  summarize(
    observations = n(),
    stations = n_distinct(id),
    first_date = min(date),
    last_date = max(date)
  ) |>
  knitr::kable()

ny_noaa |>
  summarize(
    across(
      everything(),
      ~ mean(is.na(.x)) * 100
    )
  ) |>
  pivot_longer(
    everything(),
    names_to = "Variable",
    values_to = "Missing (%)"
  ) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 2)
```
This dataset contains `r nrow(ny_noaa)` observations and `r ncol(ny_noaa)` variables, representing daily weather records from `r dplyr::n_distinct(ny_noaa$id)` stations in NY state between `r min(ny_noaa$date)` and `r max(ny_noaa$date)`. Each row represents a station-day record. 

Variables include station ID, date, precipitation, snowfall, snow depth, and daily maximum and minimum temperatures.

Missingness varies substantially across variables. Precipitation is missing in 5.62% of observations, snowfall in 14.69%, and snow depth in 22.80%. Both maximum and minimum temperatures are missing in approximately 43.71% of observations. Temperature analyses therefore rely on a substantially reduced subset of the records. Station ID and date have no missing values.

## Data cleaning

```{r}
noaa_clean =
  ny_noaa |>
  separate(
    date,
    into = c("year", "month", "day"),
    sep = "-",
    convert = TRUE,
    remove = FALSE
  ) |>
  mutate(
    tmax = as.numeric(tmax) / 10,
    tmin = as.numeric(tmin) / 10,
    prcp = prcp / 10
  )

noaa_clean |>
  filter(!is.na(snow)) |>
  count(snow, sort = TRUE) |>
  slice_head(n = 10) |>
  knitr::kable(
    col.names = c("snowfall (mm)", "number of observations")
  )
```

The date was separated into year, month, and day while retaining the original date variable. Maximum and minimum temperatures were converted to numeric values and expressed in degrees Celsius. Precipitation was converted to millimeters; snowfall and snow depth were already recorded in millimeters.

The most frequently observed snowfall value is 0 mm (2,008,508 observations), followed by 25 mm (31,022), 13 mm (23,095), and 51 mm (18,274). Zero dominates because most station-days have no snowfall. Common positive values such as 13, 25, 51, and 76 mm are approximately equivalent to 0.5, 1, 2, and 3 inches, suggesting that the recorded values reflect conversion and rounding from measurements in inches.## Average maximum temperature in January and July

## average max temperature in January and July
```{r}
noaa_monthly =
  noaa_clean |>
  filter(month %in% c(1, 7)) |>
  group_by(id, year, month) |>
  summarize(
    observed_days = sum(!is.na(tmax)),
    mean_tmax = mean(tmax, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  filter(observed_days > 0) |>
  mutate(
    month = factor(
      month,
      levels = c(1, 7),
      labels = c("January", "July")
    )
  )

ggplot(noaa_monthly, aes(x = year, y = mean_tmax)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.25, size = 0.8, color = "#2C7FB8") +
  facet_wrap(~ month, nrow = 1) +
  labs(
    title = "Average daily maximum temperature by station and year",
    subtitle = "Each point represents one station in one year",
    x = "Year",
    y = "Mean daily maximum temperature (°C)",
    caption = "Means use available daily observations; station-months with no data are excluded."
  ) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(size = 13),
    strip.text = element_text(face = "bold")
  )
```
July has much higher average daily maximum temperatures than January. Most station-level averages fall around 20–33°C in July and −10–10°C in January. Temperatures vary across stations, and many stations show similar year-to-year fluctuations, suggesting shared regional weather patterns. January shows more pronounced interannual variation than July.

There are several unusually low station-level averages, including a July value near 14°C around 1988. These observations warrant checking the underlying daily records and the number of observed days. Because monthly means use available observations, incomplete coverage may affect their comparability. The figure alone does not establish a clear long-term trend.

## Temperature relationship and snowfall distributions

```{r, fig.width=12, fig.height=6}
temperature_plot =
  noaa_clean |>
  filter(!is.na(tmin), !is.na(tmax)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = tmin, y = tmax)) +
  geom_bin_2d(bins = 70) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(
    trans = "log10",
    name = "Count"
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Daily maximum vs. minimum temperature",
    x = "Minimum temperature (°C)",
    y = "Maximum temperature (°C)"
  ) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")

snowfall_plot =
  noaa_clean |>
  filter(snow > 0, snow < 100) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = factor(year), y = snow)) +
  geom_boxplot(
    fill = "#A6CEE3",
    outlier.alpha = 0.2,
    outlier.size = 0.5
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Annual snowfall distributions",
    subtitle = "Only station-days with 0 < snowfall < 100 mm",
    x = "Year",
    y = "Snowfall (mm)"
  ) +
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_text(
      angle = 90,
      hjust = 1,
      vjust = 0.5,
      size = 8
    )
  )

(temperature_plot + snowfall_plot) +
  plot_layout(widths = c(1, 1.2)) +
  plot_annotation(tag_levels = "A")
```

Daily maximum and minimum temperatures show a strong positive association: days with higher minimum temperatures generally also have higher maximum temperatures. 

Most observations lie within a concentrated diagonal band. A few isolated records have extreme temperatures or maximum temperatures below minimum temperatures; these warrant further investigation rather than automatic removal.

Among station-days with snowfall greater than 0 and less than 100 mm, the annual distributions are broadly similar. Median snowfall is approximately 25 mm across years, and the middle 50% of observations generally spans about 13–51 mm. Some years, such as 2006 and 2010, have lower upper quartiles. These conditional distributions do not describe annual total snowfall or the frequency of snowfall days.

# Problem 2

## import & tidy the data

```{r}
nhanes_covar =
  read_csv(
    "data/nhanes_covar.csv",
    skip = 4,
    show_col_types = FALSE
  ) |>
  rename(
    seqn = SEQN,
    bmi = BMI
  ) |>
  drop_na(sex, age, bmi, education) |>
  filter(age >= 21) |>
  mutate(
    seqn = as.character(seqn),
    sex = factor(
      sex,
      levels = c(1, 2),
      labels = c("Male", "Female")
    ),
    education = factor(
      education,
      levels = c(1, 2, 3),
      labels = c(
        "Less than high school",
        "High school equivalent",
        "More than high school"
      )
    )
  )

nhanes_accel =
  read_csv(
    "data/nhanes_accel.csv",
    show_col_types = FALSE
  ) |>
  rename(seqn = SEQN) |>
  mutate(seqn = as.character(seqn)) |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = starts_with("min"),
    names_to = "minute",
    names_prefix = "min",
    names_transform = list(minute = as.integer),
    values_to = "mims"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    hour = (minute - 1) / 60
  )

nhanes =
  inner_join(
    nhanes_covar,
    nhanes_accel,
    by = "seqn"
  ) |>
  arrange(seqn, minute)

nhanes |>
  summarize(
    participants = n_distinct(seqn),
    observations = n(),
    minutes_per_participant = n() / n_distinct(seqn)
  ) |>
  knitr::kable()
```

Participants younger than 21 years and those with missing demographic information were excluded. Sex and education were encoded as factors, with education categories arranged from lower to higher attainment. The demographic and accelerometer datasets were joined by participant ID. The resulting dataset contains 228 participants and 328,320 participant-minute observations, with 1,440 activity measurements per participant.

## Participant characteristics

```{r}
nhanes_covar |>
  count(education, sex, .drop = FALSE) |>
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = sex,
    values_from = n,
    values_fill = 0
  ) |>
  mutate(Total = Male + Female) |>
  knitr::kable(
    col.names = c("Education", "Male", "Female", "Total"),
    caption = "Number of participants by education and sex"
  )
```

```{r}
ggplot(
  nhanes_covar,
  aes(x = sex, y = age, fill = sex)
) +
  geom_boxplot(
    width = 0.5,
    alpha = 0.6,
    outlier.shape = NA
  ) +
  geom_point(
    position = position_jitter(
      width = 0.12,
      height = 0,
      seed = 123
    ),
    alpha = 0.5,
    size = 1.3
  ) +
  facet_wrap(~ education, nrow = 1) +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c("Male" = "#0072B2", "Female" = "#D55E00")
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Age distributions by education and sex",
    x = "Sex",
    y = "Age (years)"
  ) +
  theme(
    legend.position = "none",
    strip.text = element_text(size = 10, face = "bold")
  )
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c("Male" = "#0072B2", "Female" = "#D55E00")
  ) 
```

The education groups include 55 participants with less than high school education, 58 with high school equivalent education, and 115 with more than high school education. The numbers of men and women are similar in the lowest and highest education groups, whereas the high school equivalent group contains more men than women (35 versus 23).

Participants with more than high school education tend to be younger, with median ages in the early 40s. In the lowest education group, median ages are approximately 60 years for both sexes. Women in the high school equivalent group tend to be older than men. These age differences should be considered when comparing activity across education groups.

## Total daily activity and age

```{r, fig.width=10, fig.height=5}
nhanes_total =
  nhanes |>
  group_by(seqn, sex, age, bmi, education) |>
  summarize(
    total_activity = sum(mims),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

ggplot(
  nhanes_total,
  aes(x = age, y = total_activity, color = sex)
) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_smooth(se = FALSE) +
  facet_wrap(~ education, nrow = 1) +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c("Male" = "#0072B2", "Female" = "#D55E00")
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Total daily activity and age by education and sex",
    x = "Age (years)",
    y = "Total daily activity (sum of minute-level MIMS)",
    color = "Sex"
  ) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

## Activity over the course of the day

```{r, fig.width=10, fig.height=5}
nhanes_time =
  nhanes |>
  group_by(education, sex, minute, hour) |>
  summarize(
    mean_mims = mean(mims),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

ggplot(
  nhanes_time,
  aes(x = hour, y = mean_mims, color = sex)
) +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.3) +
  geom_smooth(se = FALSE, span = 0.15) +
  facet_wrap(~ education, nrow = 1) +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c("Male" = "#0072B2", "Female" = "#D55E00")
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    breaks = c(0, 6, 12, 18, 24),
    limits = c(0, 24)
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Daily activity patterns by education and sex",
    x = "Hour of day",
    y = "Mean minute-level MIMS",
    color = "Sex"
  ) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

All education and sex groups show a clear daily pattern: mean activity is lowest around 4–5 a.m., rises sharply in the morning, remains elevated during the day, and declines in the evening.

In the less than high school group, activity peaks in the late morning and then gradually decreases, with broadly similar daytime patterns for men and women. In the high school equivalent group, women generally have higher mean activity during the morning and early afternoon. The more than high school group shows a more sustained daytime plateau among women, whose activity exceeds men's through most daytime hours.

These are descriptive group averages. Differences across education groups may partly reflect their different age distributions, and the curves do not imply that every participant follows the same daily pattern.

# Problem 3

## Import and clean the data

```{r}
jan_2020 =
  read_csv(
    "data/citibike/Jan 2020 Citi.csv",
    show_col_types = FALSE
  ) |>
  mutate(year = 2020, month = "January")

july_2020 =
  read_csv(
    "data/citibike/July 2020 Citi.csv",
    show_col_types = FALSE
  ) |>
  mutate(year = 2020, month = "July")

jan_2024 =
  read_csv(
    "data/citibike/Jan 2024 Citi.csv",
    show_col_types = FALSE
  ) |>
  mutate(year = 2024, month = "January")

july_2024 =
  read_csv(
    "data/citibike/July 2024 Citi.csv",
    show_col_types = FALSE
  ) |>
  mutate(year = 2024, month = "July")

citibike =
  bind_rows(jan_2020, july_2020, jan_2024, july_2024) |>
  mutate(
    year = factor(year),
    month = factor(month, levels = c("January", "July")),
    weekdays = factor(
      weekdays,
      levels = c(
        "Monday", "Tuesday", "Wednesday",
        "Thursday", "Friday", "Saturday", "Sunday"
      )
    ),
    member_casual = factor(
      member_casual,
      levels = c("casual", "member"),
      labels = c("Casual", "Member")
    ),
    rideable_type = factor(
      rideable_type,
      levels = c("classic_bike", "electric_bike"),
      labels = c("Classic", "Electric")
    )
  )

citibike |>
  count(year, month) |>
  knitr::kable(
    col.names = c("Year", "Month", "Number of rides")
  )
```

The combined dataset contains 99,485 rides and 9 variables, with each row representing one ride. It includes the ride ID, bike type, day of the week, duration in minutes, starting and ending station names, membership status, year, and month. The data cover January and July in 2020 and 2024 and represent a 1% sample of rides lasting less than four hours.

Year and month were added before combining the four files. Categorical variables were converted to factors, with months and weekdays placed in chronological order. There are 43 missing starting station names and 207 missing ending station names. These rides are retained for analyses that do not require station names.

## Ride counts by membership status

```{r}
citibike |>
  count(year, month, member_casual) |>
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = member_casual,
    values_from = n,
    values_fill = 0
  ) |>
  mutate(Total = Casual + Member) |>
  knitr::kable(
    col.names = c("Year", "Month", "Casual", "Member", "Total"),
    caption = "Sampled rides by year, month, and membership status"
  )
```

Members account for most sampled rides in all four periods. Both membership groups have more rides in July than in January in each year, and more rides in 2024 than in the corresponding month of 2020. July 2024 has the largest number of sampled rides. Casual riders also represent a larger share of rides in July than in January in both years.

## Most popular starting stations in July 2024

```{r}
citibike |>
  filter(
    year == "2024",
    month == "July",
    !is.na(start_station_name)
  ) |>
  count(start_station_name, sort = TRUE) |>
  slice_head(n = 5) |>
  knitr::kable(
    col.names = c("Starting station", "Number of rides"),
    caption = "Five most popular starting stations in July 2024"
  )
```

Pier 61 at Chelsea Piers is the most popular starting station in the July 2024 sample, with 163 rides, followed by University Pl & E 14 St with 155 rides. These rankings describe the sampled rides and may differ from rankings based on all rides.

## Median ride duration by weekday, month, and year

```{r, fig.width=10, fig.height=5}
citibike_median =
  citibike |>
  group_by(year, month, weekdays) |>
  summarize(
    median_duration = median(duration),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

ggplot(
  citibike_median,
  aes(
    x = weekdays,
    y = median_duration,
    color = month,
    group = month
  )
) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  facet_wrap(~ year, nrow = 1) +
  labs(
    title = "Median ride duration by weekday, month, and year",
    x = "Day of the week",
    y = "Median ride duration (minutes)",
    color = "Month"
  ) +
  theme(
    legend.position = "bottom",
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1)
  )
```

Median ride duration is higher in July than in January on every weekday in both years. Durations are also consistently lower in 2024 than in the corresponding month of 2020, with a particularly large difference in July.

In July 2020, median duration rises from approximately 13–14 minutes on weekdays to about 16.5 minutes on weekends. July 2024 also shows longer weekend rides, but the increase is smaller. January 2024 has relatively little weekday variation, with no consistent weekend increase. These are descriptive associations and do not establish causal effects.

## Ride duration distributions in 2024

```{r, fig.width=10, fig.height=7}
citibike |>
  filter(year == "2024") |>
  ggplot(
    aes(
      x = member_casual,
      y = duration,
      fill = rideable_type
    )
  ) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.alpha = 0.15, outlier.size = 0.5) +
  facet_grid(month ~ rideable_type) +
  scale_y_sqrt(
    breaks = c(1, 5, 10, 20, 40, 80, 160, 240)
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Ride duration distributions in 2024",
    x = "Membership status",
    y = "Ride duration (minutes; square-root scale)",
    caption = "All observations are retained."
  ) +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

Ride durations are right-skewed in all groups, with many short rides and a small number of much longer rides. Casual riders generally have higher median durations and wider interquartile ranges than members within each month and bike type.

July generally has longer typical durations than January. Among casual riders, classic-bike rides have higher medians and greater variability than electric-bike rides. Differences between bike types are smaller among members. These comparisons describe associations and do not establish that bike type or membership causes differences in duration.
